The Arctic skate (Amblyraja hyperborea) is a deepwater elasmobranch distributed across cold continental slopes of the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, where water temperatures hover near 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C]. Neonates emerge from egg cases at a total length of approximately 17 cm [Lb = approximately 17 cm], though field surveys suggest that free-swimming pups range quite narrowly between 16 and 18 cm (16-18 cm) [Lb = 16-18 cm] at the time of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of independent foraging. This relatively large size at birth reflects an extended period of yolk-dependent embryonic development within the protective capsule, a strategy common among Rajiformes that enhances early survival in food-limited environments. Data from captive rearing programs indicate that at the ambient temperature of 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C], the incubation period from egg laying through hatching lasts roughly 2.5 years [ab = roughly 2.5 years], an extraordinarily protracted embryogenesis compared with most other elasmobranchs. This lengthy pre-natal investment likely contributes to the well-developed state of the hatchlings, which immediately commence feeding on small benthic crustaceans upon emergence from the egg case.

Sexual maturation in the Arctic skate is delayed relative to many rajid congeners, with puberty attained at a total length of 45 cm [Lp = 45 cm]. Females at this size typically have a wet weight of 626 grams [Wwp = 626 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The period from birth to puberty has been estimated at approximately 11 years [tp = approximately 11 years] under the prevailing thermal regime of 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C], highlighting the extraordinarily slow pace of life history in this polar-adapted species. This late onset of reproductive capacity is consistent with the general pattern seen in other deep-sea chondrichthyans, where low metabolic rates and limited food availability impose a prolonged juvenile phase. The ultimate total length, representing the maximum recorded size for the species, has been documented at 112 cm [Li = 112 cm] from trawl surveys in the Barents Sea and Davis Strait.

Reproductive output in Amblyraja hyperborea is constrained by the same cold, resource-poor environment that governs its developmental and maturation schedules. Gravid females produce a limited number of egg cases per reproductive cycle, with the maximum reproductive rate achieved at 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C] estimated at approximately 30 pups per year [Ri = approximately 30 pups per year]. This low fecundity, combined with the protracted egg-case incubation period and the extreme delay in sexual maturation, renders the species exceptionally vulnerable to population declines from incidental bycatch in deepwater fisheries. Somatic growth following puberty remains slow, and the adult form of the species can be reliably distinguished from similar rajid species by its relatively short snout and uniformly dark dorsal coloration.

The wet weight of a fully grown, reproductively active adult represents a substantial increase over the mass at puberty. The ultimate wet weight achieved by Amblyraja hyperborea has been recorded at 11,700 grams [Wwi = 11,700 grams] in the largest females examined from sub-Arctic waters. This impressive body size supports the energetic demands of a reproductive strategy centered on producing well-yolked, capsule-enclosed eggs that require years of embryonic development before hatching. Observations of wild-caught specimens suggest that the most extreme longevity recorded for the species reaches approximately 24 years [am = approximately 24 years] in environments buffered by persistent 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C] bottom temperatures.
